ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The radius is the lateral forearm bone that articulates with the humerus and ulna, enabling forearm rotation and wrist movement. Understanding its anatomy guides diagnosis of common injuries and systemic diseases affecting bone health.

sections.p: The radius is a long bone on the thumb side of the forearm, extending from the elbow to the wrist, essential for pronation and supination.
b: Forms part of the radiocarpal joint

sections.p: It has a head, neck, shaft, and distal end with the styloid process; the distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate.
b: Distal radius forms the major wrist joint surface

sections.p: Anteriorly lies the brachioradialis and flexor carpi radialis; posteriorly the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis; interosseous membrane connects it to the ulna.
b: Muscles attach for wrist and elbow motion

sections.p: Supplied by the radial recurrent artery proximally and the dorsal and volar branches of the radial artery distally.
b: Periosteal vessels dominate shaft blood flow

sections.p: Sensory innervation of periosteum from the radial nerve (posterior) and median nerve (anterior). Motor nerves to attached muscles arise from the radial and median nerves.
Provides structural support, transmits axial load from hand to elbow, and enables pronation/supination via the proximal and distal radioulnar joints.
Fractures (distal radius, radial neck) are common after falls; osteomyelitis, especially in sickle‑cell disease; systemic bone loss (osteoporosis, TB osteitis).
b: Distal radius fracture: Colles' vs. Smith
Infection risk higher in low‑resource settings

t.b: Does it show fracture displacement? Displaced >2 mm needs reduction; normal alignment suggests a sprain
Is there occult fracture or soft‑tissue injury? Positive edema confirms fracture when X‑ray is equivocal
Is infection present? Elevated markers support osteomyelitis; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and plain film

sections.p: Assess forearm rotation, palpate the radial styloid, test wrist flexion/extension, and check for distal neurovascular status.
b: Pain on pronation suggests radial head involvement
Tender styloid indicates distal radius fracture

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of infection: fever, purulent discharge, rising CRP

faq.q: Why does a distal radius fracture cause wrist deformity?
faq.a: The distal fragment tilts dorsally (Colles') or volarly (Smith), altering the normal wrist alignment.

faq.q: Can a radial fracture affect the elbow?
faq.a: Yes, a radial head fracture impairs pronation and may cause elbow instability.

faq.q: What makes bone healing slower in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Nutritional deficiencies, delayed presentation, and limited access to imaging or surgical fixation.
